title: How We Learned Microbes Cause Disease

scenes.tts: In the eighteen forties, a hospital in Vienna had two maternity clinics. Year after year, a much larger share of mothers died of childbed fever in the First Clinic than in the Second. Childbed fever is a serious infection after giving birth. How did we figure out why?
scenes.caption: In the 1840s, a hospital in Vienna had two maternity clinics. Year after year, a much larger share of mothers died of childbed fever in the First Clinic than in the Second. Childbed fever is a serious infection after giving birth. How did we figure out why?
scenes.visual: Two labelled clinic frames; a tall red column in the First, a short one in the Second (not to scale); childbed fever chip; a big yellow Why?
scenes.narration: In the 1840s, a hospital in Vienna had two maternity clinics. Year after year, a much larger share of mothers died of childbed fever in the First Clinic than in the Second. Childbed fever is a serious infection after giving birth. How did we figure out why?

scenes.tts: The First Clinic trained doctors, who often worked with bodies. The Second Clinic trained midwives. In eighteen forty-seven, Semmelweis began washing hands in chlorine, and the death ratio, the share of mothers who died, fell. Germ theory later explained why. It says many diseases are caused by microbes. A microbe is a living thing too small to see without a microscope. A microbe that causes disease is a pathogen.

scenes.tts: A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the full disease. It works through an antigen, a substance the immune system can recognize. The body makes antibodies, proteins that stick to one antigen. The first time, the response is slow, often a week or more.
scenes.visual: Vaccine chip feeds the immune system box; pathogen blob with antigen squares; crossed-out full disease; blue antibody bars attach to the antigens; then a sketch plot of antibody level where the first rise is slow and small.
scenes.narration: A vaccine teaches the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the full disease. It works through an antigen, a substance the immune system can recognize. The body makes antibodies, proteins that stick to one antigen. The first time, the response is slow, often a week or more.

scenes.tts: During that first response, some immune cells become memory cells. Memory cells stay in the body long after. On a later exposure, memory cells recognize the antigen quickly, and memory B cells turn into cells that make large amounts of antibody. The vaccine gave the first meeting, so the real pathogen meets antibody already waiting and a faster response.
scenes.visual: The same sketch plot; a memory cells chip as the curve falls; a real pathogen marker and a faster, taller second rise.

scenes.tts: An antibiotic is a drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing. Many antibiotics block the building of the bacterial cell wall. Others jam bacterial ribosomes, the parts that make proteins. A virus has no cell wall and no ribosomes of its own. It uses the ribosomes of the cell it infects. So antibiotics do not treat colds or flu.
scenes.visual: An antibiotic chip acts on a bacterium's cell wall and ribosomes; a virus inside a host cell has neither and uses the host's ribosomes, so the antibiotic has no target.

scenes.tts: Antibiotic resistance is the ability of some bacteria to survive a drug that kills others of their kind. In a large population, a few may already carry a gene that lets them survive. The antibiotic kills or stops the sensitive ones. The resistant ones are left to multiply. This is natural selection: individuals with a helpful trait survive and reproduce more. So why do they not always succeed? Vaccines do not work perfectly in everyone, and resistant bacteria survive the drug.
scenes.visual: A schematic population of bacteria with a few resistant ones; the antibiotic removes the sensitive ones; the resistant ones fill the space; two closing chips answer the question.
